passage: The maths tests were handed back before lunch at the school in Melbourne. Soo-ah slid hers into her bag without looking at the mark again, jaw tight. Her desk partner Leila whispered, "How did you go?" and Soo-ah only shrugged. Before the bell, the teacher crouched by her desk and said quietly, "I've seen how many afternoons you stayed back to redo those problems. Your effort is showing in your working, even if not yet in the mark." Soo-ah's shoulders came down. At lunch she took out her sandwich, told Leila the score, and asked if Leila would check her working on question six.

qa.q: Where did the teacher crouch to speak with Soo-ah?
qa.a: The teacher crouched by her desk.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's change of posture suggest she felt after the teacher spoke?
qa.a: Her shoulders came down, which suggests relief and a feeling of being seen; later she shared her score and asked Leila for help, so she seemed steadier 🙂.

qa.q: How could a teacher support a student with low marks on results day?
qa.a: Quietly point to specific effort, like staying back to redo problems, so the student knows someone has noticed and believes in them.

qa.q: How might Leila have seen Soo-ah's shrug, and then the lunchtime request?
qa.a: Leila may have wondered whether to ask again, and probably felt trusted when Soo-ah shared the score and asked for help.

grounding: Illustrates a child with low marks steadied by a teacher who names her effort.

passage:
Note by Mrs Pema Dolkar, Class 5 teacher, after the unit test.
Wasim scored 11 out of 25 in the maths test, and when I handed back the papers, I saw him push his quietly into his bag and put his head down. I know how hard he has been working; I have watched him stay back three evenings this month, redoing long division. At break I called him over. 'Wasim, your mark is low. But I can see how hard you're trying, and your division is much neater than in June.' He looked up as if nobody had ever said that before. His ears went pink. 'Really, Ma'am?' 'Really.' We agreed on two more evening sessions before the next test. He walked back to class standing straighter.

qa.q: How many evenings had Wasim stayed back this month?
What did Wasim's pink ears and 'Really, Ma'am?' show?
qa.a: He felt seen and encouraged, surprised that someone had noticed his effort.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that steadied Wasim?
qa.a: She named his effort out loud, pointed out his neater division and planned more sessions with him.

qa.q: How does the teacher see Wasim's low mark?
qa.a: As one result, not the whole story; she values the hard work behind it.

grounding: A teacher's note records telling a boy with low marks that she sees his effort, and how it steadies him.

passage:
Wednesday
Diary, it's Pooja. Science results came today. I got 14 out of 30, even though I studied every night. I wanted to cry in front of everyone. But after class Dolma Ma'am stopped me at the door. She said, 'Pooja, I saw your notebook. You drew every diagram of the heart twice. That's real effort, and it shows. The marks will catch up.' I didn't know what to say. I just nodded, and my throat felt funny. Nobody had ever told me they saw me trying. At home I told Amma, and she made my favourite rasam. I still wish my marks were higher. But today didn't feel like the worst day any more. It felt like someone was on my side.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when Dolma Ma'am spoke?
qa.a: Seen and moved; Pooja's throat felt funny because nobody had noticed the trying before 🥺

qa.q: What difference did Dolma Ma'am's words make on a bad day?
qa.a: Pooja felt someone was on Pooja's side, so the day no longer felt like the worst.

qa.q: How does Dolma Ma'am see Pooja's work?
qa.a: As real effort that will show in the marks later.

grounding: A child with low marks writes about a teacher who noticed the effort, and feeling seen on a bad day.
